<div><div class="book-report__eyebrow">Book review · Korean Buddhist painting · Chosŏn dynasty · ritual and space</div><h1>조선의 불교회화</h1><p class="book-report__author">Buddhist Painting of the Chosŏn Dynasty<br>Chŏng Myŏnghŭi (정명희)</p>
<dl class="book-report__meta" aria-label="Bibliographic reference">
<div><dt>Date</dt><dd>2024</dd></div>
<div><dt>Publisher</dt><dd>사회평론아카데미</dd></div>
<div><dt>Language</dt><dd>Korean</dd></div>
<div><dt>Field</dt><dd>Buddhist art history · Korean painting · Chosŏn · ritual history</dd></div>
<div><dt>Type</dt><dd>Scholarly monograph</dd></div>
<div><dt>Reference</dt><dd>ISBN 979-11-6707-150-7 · 496 pp.</dd></div>
</dl>
<div class="book-report__domain"><strong>Central question:</strong> What happens to our understanding of Chosŏn Buddhist painting when we stop treating it as an autonomous image and instead reconstruct its place in the monastery, its ritual altar and the actions performed around it?</div></div></div></header>
<div class="book-report__nav-wrap"><nav class="book-report__shell book-report__nav" aria-label="Review contents"><a href="#pourquoi-lire">Why read it?</a><a href="#comprendre">What it explains</a><a href="#apports">Contribution</a><a href="#reperes">Key works</a><a href="#these">Author’s argument</a><a href="#changement">What it changes</a><a href="#limites">Limits</a><a href="#public">For whom?</a><a href="#verdict">Verdict</a></nav></div>
<section class="book-report__section" id="pourquoi-lire"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">01 · Essential</div><h2>Why read this book?</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><p>This book matters for Buddhist art history because it changes the basic question. Rather than asking only what a painting represents, Chŏng Myŏnghŭi asks <em>where</em> it was installed, <em>before whom</em>, <em>during which ritual</em>, and <em>to produce what religious effect</em>. A painting therefore ceases to be a flat image detached from its surroundings and becomes part of a system formed by sculpture, altar, architecture, officiants, worshippers and movement.</p><p>This approach clarifies why Chosŏn main halls came to contain multiple paintings with distinct ritual functions, why visual types could serve differently depending on location, and why monumental <em>kwaebul</em> (掛佛) moved outside the building to organize large public ceremonies. For Korean Buddhist art, it provides a stronger way of seeing objects too often studied only through iconography or style.</p></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="comprendre"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">02 · Knowledge</div><h2>What the book helps us understand</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><ul class="book-report__keypoints"><li><strong>A Buddhist painting has a function, not only an iconography.</strong> Meaning changes with altar, hall, ceremony and the viewer’s physical relation to the image.</li><li><strong>The main hall is a structured ritual environment.</strong> The development of a three-altar system explains why several paintings could form a coherent ensemble in one building.</li><li><strong>Architecture shapes images.</strong> Statue size, the rear altar wall and actual sightlines affect composition.</li><li><strong>Paintings can move.</strong> When rituals expanded into the courtyard, sacred images moved with them; the monumental <em>kwaebul</em> made divine presence visible to a larger community.</li><li><strong>Ritual manuals are art-historical sources.</strong> They reconstruct the functions of altars and explain categories of paintings that stylistic analysis alone cannot adequately interpret.</li></ul></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="apports"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">03 · Perspective</div><h2>Contribution to art history, Buddhism and Asian history</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><p><strong>For art history</strong>, the major contribution is methodological: style and iconography are reinserted into concrete conditions of installation and visibility. The relationship between sculpture and the painting behind the altar shows that composition was not determined by doctrine alone; it also responded to how an image would actually be seen.</p><p><strong>For Buddhist studies</strong>, paintings emerge as active components of ritual efficacy. They materialize invoked presences, distinguish ritual altars and participate in ceremonies directed toward the living, the dead and protective deities.</p><p><strong>For Korean and East Asian history</strong>, the book highlights a characteristic Chosŏn solution: the main hall could operate as a polyvalent ritual space coordinating several visual and liturgical systems. This invites comparison with Koryŏ, China and Japan without reducing Chosŏn practice to mere continuity.</p></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="reperes"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">04 · Key references</div><h2>Works, ritual devices and sources to remember</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><ul class="book-report__entities"><li><strong>Chingwansa (진관사) and the Suryukchae (수륙재)</strong><span>Records connected with Water-Land rituals provide important evidence for the formation of multi-altar ritual arrangements.</span></li><li><strong>Hubult’aeng (후불탱)</strong><span>The painting hung behind the main statue is crucial for understanding the interaction of sculpture, painting, sightlines and the upper altar.</span></li><li><strong>Kwanŭm posaldo (관음보살도)</strong><span>Avalokiteśvara paintings behind the rear altar wall demonstrate that less visible zones of the hall could possess precise ritual functions.</span></li><li><strong>Samjang posaldo (삼장보살도)</strong><span>This type helps explain the ritual importance of the middle altar and the organization of deity groups in Chosŏn liturgy.</span></li><li><strong>Kamnodo (감로도)</strong><span>The “nectar painting” is central to the lower altar, rites for the dead and the visualization of ritual feeding.</span></li><li><strong>Kwaebul (掛佛)</strong><span>The monumental hanging painting encapsulates one of the book’s strongest arguments: when ritual moves, the image moves and reorganizes monastic space with it.</span></li></ul></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="these"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">05 · Argument</div><h2>The author’s central argument</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><p class="book-report__thesis">Chosŏn Buddhist painting cannot be understood correctly when separated from space and ritual. Iconography, scale, placement and even composition respond to functions performed within concrete ritual arrangements. The history of these paintings is therefore also a history of changing main halls, the formation of ritual altars and the extension of ceremonies into outdoor space.</p></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="changement"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">06 · Significance</div><h2>What this book changes in our understanding</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><p>After this book, it becomes difficult to study Korean Buddhist painting only through a catalogue photograph or museum display. Many works were designed to be partly hidden by sculpture, suspended at a specific height, moved for ceremonies or encountered collectively in temporarily transformed spaces. Their visual form was partly produced by these conditions.</p><p>The second change is historiographical. The density of paintings in Chosŏn halls no longer needs to be described as decorative excess or as evidence of doctrinal decline. It can instead be read as the coherent outcome of a ritual system. That correction matters for the history of religious architecture as much as for painting.</p></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="limites"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">07 · Critical reading</div><h2>Limits of the book</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><div class="book-report__limits">The book’s methodological strength is also its principal limit. Its emphasis on function, space and ritual leaves comparatively less room for material analysis of pigments and supports, the organization of monk-painter workshops, conservation history and the economics of commissions. The corpus is strongly centered on Chosŏn, especially ritual systems that become most legible in the later period; comparisons with China, Japan and Koryŏ mainly sharpen Korean specificity rather than build an evenly transregional history. Finally, the Korean-language text and specialized ritual terminology make the book demanding for readers without Korean.</div></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="public"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">08 · Audience</div><h2>Who is this book for?</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><div class="book-report__audience"><div><strong>Beginner</strong><span>Highly informative but demanding without prior knowledge of Korean Buddhism and major ritual painting types.</span></div><div><strong>Student</strong><span>Excellent for learning how to connect iconography, architecture, ritual texts and actual conditions of use.</span></div><div><strong>Researcher</strong><span>Important for Korean Buddhist painting, Chosŏn ritual, main-hall studies and religious spatiality.</span></div><div><strong>Informed reader</strong><span>Especially useful for readers visiting Korean monasteries who want to understand why images occupy their particular locations.</span></div></div></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="verdict"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">09 · Conclusion</div><h2>Verdict</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><div class="book-report__verdict"><div class="book-report__verdict-label">Recommendation</div><strong>Essential for the study of Korean Buddhist art</strong><p>Its key achievement is to restore paintings to the environments for which they were made. A Buddhist image is not merely an iconography to identify: it acts within a space alongside statues, altars, officiants and communities. For Chosŏn studies, this is an exceptionally productive analytical framework.</p></div></div></div></section>
